devotionals.title: Taught by God, Leading to God
devotionals.quote: These two must be joined together because we cannot speak concerning God without God; so that it may be termed the science which is originally from God, objectively treats concerning and terminatively flows into and leads to him … So this nomenclature embraces the twofold principle of theology: one of being, which is God; the other of knowing, which is his word. … In the third and most proper sense, it denotes "a system or body of doctrine concerning God and divine things revealed by him for his own glory and the salvation of men." In this sense, we use it here.
devotionals.reflection:
Turretin is defending a single word here, and the defense turns into a confession. He will not let theology mean talk about God that begins with us. You cannot speak of God without God, he says, because nobody has climbed up to find him. He has to speak first.

That should change how you open the Bible this morning. A student can master a subject and walk away unchanged, and Turretin knows it. His own work runs to three thick volumes of careful argument, and he still says theology ends by leading you to God. If your reading has become a duty to finish, or a stock of answers for the next argument, you have stopped short of where the road goes.

Paul had just spent three chapters on the hardest questions in Romans, and he ended them in worship. Let your study end the same way.
devotionals.prayer: Father, you spoke before I ever asked. Forgive me for the mornings I have treated your Word as one more thing to get through. Teach me by your Spirit as I read, and do not let me stop at knowing the right answers. Bring me to Christ, and bring me back to you. Amen.

devotionals.title: Why God Makes Himself Known
devotionals.quote: Many things prove that there is a theology. (1) The nature and goodness of God who, since he is the best, is most communicative of himself. He cannot communicate himself more suitably to a rational creature and in a manner more fitting to human nature than by the knowledge and love of himself. (2) The consent of people and the universal, innate desire to know God which must be for some purpose. For although they have shamefully wandered from true theology, yet the very fact of their seeking it proves the existence of such a theology. … (3) The design of creation; for God made rational creatures with this intention—that he might be recognized and worshipped by them, which cannot be done without theology. … (5) The necessity of salvation; for as man is appointed for a supernatural end, he must necessarily have presented to him supernatural means for reaching that end. Now this is no other than faith which absolutely requires the knowledge of God.
devotionals.reflection:
Turretin's first proof has nothing to do with human need. He starts with what God is like. The highest good gives itself away, and the best gift God can give a creature made to think and love is the knowledge of himself.

His second proof is quieter. Every nation has had its priests and its shrines. They wandered badly, but the searching shows that people were made for something. You know that restlessness yourself, on the days when nothing you own or have achieved quite answers it.

In John 17, on the night before he died, Jesus prayed to the Father and described eternal life as knowing the Father and the Son. So the knowledge of God is more than a preparation for life. It is the life you were made for, and it has already begun in you.
devotionals.prayer: Lord, you did not leave me to guess at you. You have made yourself known in your Son. When I am restless this morning, turn me back to you, and let me want to know you more than I want anything you could give me. Amen.

devotionals.title: No Saving Religion Without Christ
devotionals.quote: The question is not whether natural theology is useful to men, for we acknowledge its various ends and uses: (1) as a witness of the goodness of God towards sinners unworthy even of these remains of light (Acts 14:16,17; Jn. 1:5); (2) as a bond of external discipline among men to prevent the world from becoming utterly corrupt (Rom. 2:14, 15); (3) as a subjective condition in man for the admission of the light of grace because God does not appeal to brutes and stocks, but to rational creatures; (4) as an incitement to the search for this more illustrious revelation (Acts 14:27); (5) to render men inexcusable (Rom. 1:20) both in this life, in the judgment of an accusing conscience (Rom. 2:15) and, in the future life, in the judgment which God shall judge concerning the secrets of men (Rom. 2:16). Rather the question is Is it by itself sufficient for salvation, and was the design of God in that revelation the salvation of those to whom it is made? This we deny. … There can be no saving religion without Christ and faith in him (Jn. 3:16; 17:3; Acts 4:11,12; 1 Cor. 3:11; Heb. 11:6). But Christ is revealed nowhere except in the gospel; nor is faith given without the word, since it comes by hearing (Rom. 10:17). … For since the Scriptures testify that Christ is the only way of salvation (without whom no one can come to the Father), it is criminal to suppose an extraordinary way without him.
devotionals.reflection:
Turretin gives the light of nature its due. It restrains the world, it testifies to God's kindness, and it can stir a person to look further. A sunrise is a real gift. But a sunrise cannot tell a guilty person how to be forgiven.

The Westminster Confession opens the same way. Creation shows enough of God to leave us without excuse, and it does not show enough to save.

Turretin's last line is severe, and he means it to be. The kindness in it is easy to miss. If salvation came by some private road, nobody would need to be sent, and no one would need to preach. Paul reasons the other way in Romans 10: people must hear, so someone must go.

Think of how the gospel reached you. A parent, a pastor, a friend, a book left on a shelf. Somebody opened their mouth, and God used it.
devotionals.prayer: Thank you, Lord, for the people who told me about Christ. I do not deserve to have heard. Give me courage to speak to those around me, and bless the preaching of your Word in my church this Lord's Day. Amen.

devotionals.title: As Much as He Has Been Pleased to Reveal
devotionals.quote: It is not necessary for the habit of a science so to comprehend its object as to have a perfect knowledge of whatever belongs to it. It is sufficient if it knows many things concerning it and can draw deductions from its principles. Therefore, a science need not necessarily be equal to its subject by an exact and arithmetical equality. It suffices if it is equal according to some proportion of equality which is found in theology. For theology treats of God and his infinite perfections, not as knowing them in an infinite but in a finite manner; nor absolutely as much as they can be known in themselves, but as much as he has been pleased to reveal them. So theology may be properly said to equal its object according to the formal relation of revelation, not by equalling God himself, but only the revelation given by him.
devotionals.reflection:
The scholastic language can hide how comforting this is. Turretin is asking how a finite mind could ever do theology at all. His answer is that you do not have to contain God to know him truly. Your knowledge only has to match what he has chosen to say.

So you can stop in two places. You can stop being anxious that you have not worked out every question about providence, or evil, or the future. God has not told you everything, and he has not asked you to know it. You can also stop treating revelation as vague. What he has said, he has really said.

Moses makes the same division in a single verse. Some things stay with God. Others he has handed down to his people from one generation to the next, so that they will obey them. Most of us spend too much time on the first and too little on the second.
devotionals.prayer: Lord, you are greater than my mind can hold, and I am glad of it. Keep me from prying into what you have kept to yourself, and from neglecting what you have plainly said. Make me content with your Word and quick to obey it. Amen.

devotionals.title: Light and Heat
devotionals.quote: We consider theology to be neither simply theoretical nor simply practical, but partly theoretical, partly practical, as that which at the same time connects the theory of the true with the practice of the good. Yet it is more practical than theoretical. … There is no mystery proposed to our contemplation as an object of faith which does not excite us to the worship of God or which is not prerequisite for its proper performance. … The form embraces the essence of true religion, and demands the knowledge and worship of God which are connected together inseparably (as in the sun, light and heat can never be separated from each other). So neither can that knowledge of God be true unless attended by practice (Jn. 13:17; 1 Jn. 2:5). Nor can that practice be right and saving which is not directed by knowledge (Jn. 17:3).
devotionals.reflection:
A sun that gave light without heat would not be the sun. That is Turretin's picture of true religion, and it is a good one to check yourself against.

He had real opponents on both sides. The Socinians wanted practice without doctrine, so that the Trinity and the incarnation could be quietly dropped. Others treated theology as a thing to contemplate. Turretin will have neither, and his claim is bolder than a compromise. Every doctrine in Scripture, even the most mysterious, is there to lead you to worship.

Reformed Christians usually lean one way. We can know a great deal and love very little. Others have warmth and no idea what they believe. John's first letter gives a plain test: the person who says he knows God and ignores his commandments has not told the truth.

Which way do you lean this morning?
devotionals.prayer: Father, join what I know to how I live. Where I have light and no heat, warm my heart. Where I have zeal without knowledge, teach me. Show me one thing to obey today, and give me grace to do it. Amen.

devotionals.title: Grace Does Not Destroy Nature
devotionals.quote: The orthodox occupy a middle ground. They do not confound theology with sound philosophy as the parts of a whole; nor do they set them against each other as contraries, but subordinate and compound them as subordinates which are not at variance with, but mutually assist each other. Philo Judaeus and, after him, the fathers appropriately illustrated this by the allegory of Sarah and Hagar—the mistress and servant. Theology rules over philosophy, and this latter acts as a handmaid to and subserves the former. They acknowledge that it has many and various uses in theology which must be accurately distinguished from its many abuses. … Although every truth cannot be demonstrated by reason (the boundaries of truth being much more widely extended than those of reason), yet no lie against the truth can be sheltered under the protection of true reason, nor can one truth be destroyed by another (although one may transcend and surpass the other) because whatever the one may be—whether below, according to or above reason, and apprehended by the senses, the intellect or faith—it has come from no other source than God, the parent of truth. So grace does not destroy nature, but makes it perfect. Nor does the supernatural revelation abrogate the natural, but makes it sure.
devotionals.reflection:
Christians have often felt they had to choose between faith and a working mind. Turretin refuses the choice. All truth has one source, so no real truth can contradict another. Some truths go beyond what reason could find, but none of them is a lie told against it.

Notice the order, though. Theology is the mistress and philosophy the servant. The danger Paul warns about in Colossians 2 is the servant taking over, when ideas built on human speculation start deciding what God is allowed to have said. He has no quarrel with thinking. He places all wisdom in Christ.

You need not be afraid of a hard question or a clever objection. If something is true, it belongs to God already. Keep the order right, and keep thinking.
devotionals.prayer: God of all truth, thank you that your Word cannot be overturned. I bring you the question that troubles me most, and I ask for honesty and patience with it. Take my thoughts captive to Christ, and keep my reason in its proper place. Amen.

devotionals.title: The Foundation
devotionals.quote: The orthodox hold the mean between both. As they necessarily build upon some fundamentals, so they neither restrict them too closely, nor extend them too far. … As in a house that is the foundation which has such a position that the house can neither be erected nor stand without it, so in religion that is the foundation upon which the whole of religion depends and it standing, religion stands; removed, religion falls. … Although all the truths revealed in Scripture are necessary to be believed as divine and infallible, yet they are not all equally necessary and the amplitude and extension of faith must be accurately distinguished here from its necessity. Not everything which belongs to the amplitude of faith must therefore belong to its necessity. All truths are not of the same weight.
devotionals.reflection:
All truths are not of the same weight. That sentence could save a lot of churches a lot of grief.

Turretin wrote in a century of fierce controversy, and he was no doctrinal minimalist. He has just finished saying that the Socinians cut away too much. But he also rebukes those who turn every disagreement into a heresy. Some doctrines hold up the house. Others are the furniture. You should care about the furniture, and you should know the difference.

He goes on to say that the foundation is, first of all, Christ himself. Paul uses the same image in 1 Corinthians 3. Much of what you build in a lifetime may be burned up on the last day, and the builder will still be saved, because the foundation does not burn.

Ask yourself what you have been treating as the foundation lately. Then ask what you have been fighting about.
devotionals.prayer: Lord Jesus, you are the foundation, and nothing I have built can add to that. Give me firmness where your truth is at stake and gentleness where it is not. Keep me from pride in my own building, and let my work this week be worth keeping. Amen.

devotionals.title: Our Only Teacher
devotionals.quote: Christ is our only teacher (Mt. 23:8) in such a sense as that the ministry of the word is not thereby excluded, but necessarily included because now in it only he addresses us and by it instructs us. Christ is not set in opposition to the Scriptures; rather he is set in opposition to the false teachers of the Pharisees who ambitiously assumed the authority due to Christ alone. … Although the Scriptures formally are of no personal use to those who cannot read (analphabêtous), yet materially they serve for their instruction and edification much as the doctrines preached in the church are drawn from this source.
devotionals.reflection:
Some people in Turretin's day claimed that since Christ is our only teacher, we need no written book and no preacher. He answers that this gets things backward. The written Word and the ministry are how Christ teaches now.

There is a pastoral note in the second part that is easy to pass over. Plenty of believers in his day could not read. Turretin does not treat them as second-class. The Scriptures reached them through the pulpit, and what was preached came from the same source.

The letter to the Hebrews opens by saying that God, after speaking in many ways through the prophets, has spoken at last in his Son. When you read this morning, you are hearing that same voice. You do not need a sign or a private impression to hear from Christ. Open the book.
devotionals.prayer: Lord Jesus, you are my teacher. Speak to me this morning through your Word. Thank you for those who have opened it to me, and bless my pastor as he prepares to preach. Make me a ready and teachable hearer. Amen.

devotionals.title: The Word That Cannot Lie
devotionals.quote: The reasons are: (1) The Scriptures are inspired of God (theopneustos, 2 Tim. 3:16). The word of God cannot lie (Ps. 19:8, 9; Heb. 6:18); cannot pass away and be destroyed (Mt. 5:18); shall endure forever (1 Pet. 1:25); and is truth itself (Jn. 17:17). For how could such things be predicated of it, if it contained dangerous contradictions, and if God suffered either the sacred writers to err and to slip in memory, or incurable blemishes to creep into it? … The principal arguments for the integrity of the Scriptures and the purity of the sources are four. (1) The chief of these is the providence of God (who as he wished to provide for our faith by inspiring the sacred writers as to what they should write, and by preserving the Scriptures against the attempts of enemies who have left nothing untried that they might destroy them), so he should keep them pure and uncorrupted in order that our faith might always have a firm foundation.
devotionals.reflection:
Turretin's argument is short. The Bible's character depends on its author. If God cannot lie, what he has breathed out cannot deceive you.

He adds a second point that deserves more attention. The God who inspired the Scriptures also kept them. Copies burned, emperors banned them, and scribes made their small mistakes, and still the Word reached you. Turretin names the care of the scribes and the great number of manuscripts, but he puts God's providence first. Your Bible on the table this morning is the result of a very long act of faithfulness.

In Psalm 19 David loves the law. He talks about it the way a hungry man talks about bread. Only a trustworthy Word can be loved that way, and you cannot rest your whole weight on something you half suspect.
devotionals.prayer: Faithful God, you have kept your Word through every age, and you have put it in my hands. Forgive my doubts and my carelessness with so great a gift. Let me love it, and let me lean on your promises today. Amen.

devotionals.title: In the Word and in the Heart
devotionals.quote: For as two things are necessary to the generating of faith (the presentation of truth in the word and the application of it in the heart), the Holy Spirit operates in both (i.e., in the word and in the heart). … Hence, we must understand by the Holy Spirit, the Spirit's speaking both in the word and in the heart. For the same Spirit who acts objectively in the word by presenting the truth, operates efficiently in the heart also by impressing that truth upon our minds. Thus he is very different from a Spirit of enthusiasm. … For the Spirit that testifies in us concerning the inspiration of the Scriptures is not peculiar to individuals with regard to the principle and origin. Rather he is common to the whole church and so to all believers in whom he works the same faith, although he is such subjectively with regard to each individual because he is given separately to each believer.
devotionals.reflection:
How do you know the Bible is God's Word? Rome answered that the church tells you. The enthusiasts of Turretin's day answered that the Spirit told them, apart from Scripture and sometimes against it. Turretin rejects both, and he follows Calvin in doing so.

The Spirit works in two places. He gave the Word, and he opens the heart to receive it. Your conviction is personal, because the Spirit is given to you. It is not private, because the same Spirit works the same faith in the whole church. So you should be wary of any inner voice that tells you what no believer before you has ever heard.

Paul remembered how the gospel came to Thessalonica. It came as words, and it also came with power and deep conviction. That is what you are asking for each morning before you read.
devotionals.prayer: Holy Spirit, you gave this Word. Open my heart to receive it. Press it home, so that I am more than informed. Keep me from trusting my own impressions, and join me in faith to all your people. Amen.

devotionals.title: The Sun Still Rises
devotionals.quote: If any deny the inspiration of the Scriptures, it is not because the object in itself is not known or understandable, but because they are destitute of a well-disposed faculty. To them the gospel is hid because Satan has blinded their eyes (2 Cor. 4:4); as some deny God (who is most capable of being known) because they are fools, or do not see the sun because they are blind; as the blind woman in Seneca complained that the sun did not rise. Yet notwithstanding this the sun always sends forth his rays, which are perceived per se by those who have eyes.
devotionals.reflection:
Seneca's blind woman complained that the sun had not risen. Turretin uses her to make a sober point. When someone cannot see the truth of Scripture, the fault lies in the eyes.

This should steady you. A confident unbeliever can make you feel as if the Bible has been found out. It has not. People have denied the sun's light before, and it went on shining.

It should also humble you, because you were that woman. Nothing in your intelligence or your upbringing opened your eyes. Paul says in 2 Corinthians 4 that the same God who made the first light made the good news shine for you. Your faith has no room for superiority.

So pray for the blind and do not sneer at them. Argument has its place, but the need runs deeper than argument can reach.
devotionals.prayer: Lord, I was blind and you gave me sight. Keep me from looking down on anyone who cannot yet see. I bring to you the person I most want to know you. Do for them what you have done for me. Amen.

devotionals.title: Search the Scriptures
devotionals.quote: The canon of the Old Testament suffices for faith and practice, and those sacred writings in which Timothy was instructed from his childhood (when the New Testament canon was not complete) could make him wise (sophisai) unto salvation (2 Tim. 3:15,16). And if "the man of God" (i.e., the minister of the gospel) may be thoroughly furnished by them unto every good work, much more are they useful and necessary to the faith of a private man and the direction of his life. … Christ directs the Jews to search the Scriptures (Jn. 5:39) that from them they might have eternal life. This was not said to the Jews indicatively only, but also imperatively. The design of Christ was to lead the Jews to the reading of the Scriptures, as the means of bringing them to a knowledge of himself and as an unexceptionable witness of himself. Even if Christ had spoken indicatively, it would have amounted to the same thing because he approved that practice.
devotionals.reflection:
Many Christians read the Old Testament as background. Turretin had to argue against those who said it no longer belonged to believers at all, and his answer is worth hearing. The only Bible Timothy had as a child was the Old Testament, and it made him wise for salvation.

The men in John 5 show the opposite danger. They studied the Scriptures with great care and missed the person standing in front of them. It is possible to read closely and still miss the point. Jesus does not tell them to read less. He sends them back, because those books speak of him.

When you turn to Leviticus or Isaiah, read as someone looking for Christ. Ask what this passage shows you of your need, and how it points to the one who answered it.
devotionals.prayer: Lord Jesus, keep my reading from becoming an end in itself. Open the Old Testament to me and show me yourself there. Let me come to you and live, and not only to the page. Amen.

devotionals.title: The End of the Law
devotionals.quote: That which was in no way given by Christ, either mediately or immediately, does not pertain to Christians. But the law which was given by Moses was given also by Christ; by Moses as a servant, by Christ as the Lord. … Christ is called the "end of the law" (Rom. 10:4) both because he was the mark at which the whole law aimed and because he was its perfection (teleiösis) and fulfillment, not by abrogating every use of it, but by fulfilling its predictions and obeying it both in himself (by acting and suffering) and in his people (by writing it on their hearts). Hence he says, "I am not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil it" (Mt. 5:17).
devotionals.reflection:
It is easy to think of Moses and Christ as two opposite voices. Turretin says the law came from both, from Moses as a servant and from Christ as the Lord. The one who gave it at Sinai is the one who kept it in Galilee.

Notice the two places where he says the law is fulfilled. Christ fulfilled it in himself, by obeying it and by bearing its curse. He also fulfills it in his people, by writing it on their hearts.

Both have to be held together. If you forget the first, you will try to earn what has already been given. If you forget the second, you will treat grace as permission. The Westminster Confession devotes its nineteenth chapter to this. The law cannot justify you, and it remains the rule of your life.

Your obedience this morning is a response to a debt already paid.
devotionals.prayer: Lord Jesus, you kept the law in my place and you bore what I owed. I have no righteousness but yours. Write your law on my heart, and let me obey you today out of gratitude. Amen.

devotionals.title: From Babel to Zion
devotionals.quote: The reading and contemplation of the Scriptures is enjoined upon men of all languages, therefore the translation of it into the native tongues is necessary. Since men speak different languages and are not all familiar with those two in which it was first written, it cannot be understood by them unless translated; it comes as the same thing to say nothing at all and to say what nobody can understand. But here it happens by the wonderful grace of God that the division of tongues (which formerly was the sign of a curse) becomes now the proof of a heavenly blessing. What was introduced to destroy Babel is now used to build up the mystical Zion. … The gospel is preached in all languages; therefore it can and ought to be translated into them. The consequence holds good from the preached to the written word because there is the same reason for both and the same arguments (which induced the apostles to preach in the native tongue) prove the necessity of versions.
devotionals.reflection:
This was a live fight in Turretin's world. Rome held to the Latin Bible. Men had been burned for putting Scripture into English. The Reformed answered that a Word nobody can understand might as well be silent.

Then Turretin lifts his eyes, and the argument turns into wonder. Languages were scattered at Babel as a judgment. At Pentecost those same languages carried the great deeds of God to people from every nation. What had been a curse became a means of grace. Only God rescues a thing in that way.

The Bible in your hand exists because of that reversal, and because of translators who paid dearly for it. It was never meant to be kept by scholars. It was meant for a plowboy, a seamstress, and you.
devotionals.prayer: Father, thank you for giving me your Word in my own language, and for those who suffered to bring it. Do not let me leave it closed. Remember the peoples who still wait for it, and send your gospel to them. Amen.

devotionals.title: Helps Along the Way
devotionals.quote: The question does not concern the perspicuity which does not exclude the means necessary for interpretation (i.e., the internal light of the Spirit, attention of mind, the voice and ministry of the church, sermons and commentaries, prayer and watchfulness). For we hold these means not only to be useful, but also necessary ordinarily. We only wish to proscribe the darkness which would prevent the people from reading the Scriptures as hurtful and perilous and compel them to have recourse to tradition when they might rest in the Scriptures alone. … The question then comes to this—whether the Scriptures are so plain in things essential to salvation (not as to the things delivered, but as to the mode of delivery; not as to the subject, but the object) that without the external aid of tradition or the infallible judgment of the church, they may be read and understood profitably by believers. The papists deny this; we affirm it.
devotionals.reflection:
When the Reformers said Scripture was clear, they did not mean you could read it alone and need nobody. Look at Turretin's list: the light of the Spirit, an attentive mind, the church, sermons, commentaries, prayer and watchfulness. He calls them necessary.

What he refuses is the claim that ordinary believers need an infallible interpreter standing between them and the text. You may open this book and be fed.

Nehemiah 8 shows how the two fit together. Ezra read the law aloud to the whole assembly, and teachers among the Levites explained what had been heard. Everyone was there, and teachers served them.

Your commentaries and your pastor are helps of that kind. They serve you, and they answer to the same Word you are reading. Use them gratefully, and use them with your Bible open.
devotionals.prayer: Lord, give me an attentive mind this morning. Thank you for the teachers who have helped me, living and dead. Keep me humble enough to be taught, and keep my trust in your Word above every human voice. Amen.

devotionals.title: Open My Eyes
devotionals.quote: The ignorance and blindness of man are not to be compounded with the obscurity of the Scriptures. The former is often pressed upon the Scriptures, but it is not so, nor can the latter be legitimately inferred from the former no more than that the sun is obscure because it cannot be seen by a blind man. Hence if David and other believers desire their eyes to be opened that they may see wonderful things out of the law, it does not therefore prove the obscurity of the Scriptures, but only the ignorance of men. The question here is not Do men need the light of the Holy Spirit in order to understand the Scriptures? (which we willingly grant); but Are the Scriptures obscure to a believing and illuminated man? Again, illumination may be either theoretical or practical, in its first stage or in its increase. David does not properly seek the former, but the latter.
devotionals.reflection:

devotionals.title: To the Diligent Seeker
devotionals.quote: Although the Scriptures must be searched (Jn. 5:39), it does not follow that they are everywhere obscure even in things essential to salvation. First because we do not say that they are perspicuous to everyone, but only to the attentive mind and diligent seeker. Moreover there is need of scrutiny because they are perspicuous to the one who searches, for the most evident things will be obscure to the cursory and careless reader. Second we do not deny that the Scriptures have their adyta ("heights") and depths (bathë) of mysteries to be fathomed only by the most laborious study and persevering efforts. But then there are many other things (and these essential) which readily strike the eyes of believers.
devotionals.reflection:
A child can find the gospel in Scripture, and a scholar can spend his whole life and never reach the bottom. Turretin holds both together. What you must know to be saved lies open. The rest repays digging.

One line is a little uncomfortable. The most evident things will be obscure to the cursory and careless reader. So a person can read the plainest chapter in the Bible and receive nothing, because he was hurrying to finish it.

Proverbs 2 describes wisdom as something you go after the way a man goes after buried silver. Nobody finds treasure by glancing across the field.

You probably have only a few minutes this morning. That is fine. Spend them slowly on one verse, and let it be enough. When you meet a hard passage, stay with it a while before you move on.
devotionals.prayer: Lord, forgive my hurried reading. Slow me down this morning. Make me patient with what is hard and thankful for what is plain, and let me treasure your Word above the things I chase after. Amen.

devotionals.title: More Reason to Read
devotionals.quote: If men abuse the Scriptures, this does not happen per se, but accidentally from the perversity of those who wrongfully wrest them to their own destruction. Otherwise (if on account of the abuse the use should be prohibited), the Scriptures ought to be taken away not only from the laity, but also from the teachers who abuse them far more. For heresies usually arise not from the common people and the unlearned, but from ecclesiastics. … If errors can arise from the Scriptures improperly understood, so far from keeping them from their perusal, this ought the rather to excite them to searching. Thus, properly understanding them, they may be able to confute such errors. … The liberty of reading the Scriptures does not take away either oral instruction or pastoral direction or other helps necessary to understanding. It only opposes the tyranny of those who do not wish the darkness of their errors to be dissipated by the light of the divine word.
devotionals.reflection:
Rome's argument sounded cautious: ordinary people will misread the Bible, so keep it from them. Turretin's reply has a dry wit. If misuse is the test, take it from the clergy first, because heresies have usually come from them.

He is careful in the other direction too. Liberty to read does not cancel the need for pastors and teachers. It only ends the tyranny of keeping people in the dark.

Peter admits, in his second letter, that some things in Paul are hard and that unstable people twist them. His remedy is to grow in Christ, in his favor and in knowing him. He never suggests reading less.

You may know someone who was harmed by a bad reading of the Bible. You may have done some harm with one yourself. The cure for bad reading is better reading, done in the company of the church.
devotionals.prayer: Father, thank you that your Word is open to me. Guard me from twisting it to suit myself. Help me grow in Christ, and keep me close to your church. Amen.

devotionals.title: One Sense, Many Uses
devotionals.quote: That the Scriptures have only one sense is evident: (1) from the unity of truth—because truth is only one and simple and therefore cannot admit many senses without becoming uncertain and ambiguous; (2) from the unity of form—because there is only one essential form of any one thing (now the sense is the form of the Scriptures); (3) from the perspicuity of the Scriptures, which cannot allow various foreign and diverse senses. … Distinguish the sense of the Scriptures from their application—the sense is only one, whether simple (in the histories, precepts and prophecies openly proposed) or composite (in the typical); whether proper (enunciated in proper words) or figurative (in figurative words). … Thus allegory, anagogy and tropology are not so much diverse senses as applications of one literal sense.
devotionals.reflection:
Medieval interpreters found four senses in a text. Turretin says a passage has one, and that one sense may be plain, figurative, or typical, as the Holy Spirit intended it.

This matters at your breakfast table. A text means what God meant by it. It does not mean whatever strikes you this morning. The question "What does this verse mean to me?" can quietly replace the Word of God with your own mood.

Turretin also leaves room for you. One meaning can have many applications. The same verse can teach you on Monday, correct you on Thursday, and comfort you at a graveside. Paul tells Timothy that all Scripture is useful in just these ways.

So read in that order. First ask what the passage says. Then ask what it requires of you and what it promises you.
devotionals.prayer: Lord, teach me to listen before I speak. Keep me from reading my own thoughts into your Word. Show me what this passage means, and then show me what you would have me believe and do today. Amen.

devotionals.title: God, His Own Interpreter
devotionals.quote: The threefold judge must be accurately distinguished here. First is the supreme and autocratic (autokratorikos), which judges by legislative and absolute authority after the manner of the highest prince, which enacts laws and from which there is no appeal. Second is the subordinate (hypêretikos) or ministerial, which interprets the laws after the manner of a public minister. Third is an idiomatic (idiötikos) or private, which both from the laws and from their interpretation judges in the way of private discretion. The first gives a judgment of final and absolute decision. The second gives a judgment of public determination, but subordinate and in accordance with the laws. The third gives a judgment of private discretion without any public authority. Here we dispute not about the ministerial and private judgment, but the supreme and infallible. … As a prince must interpret his own law, so also God must be the interpreter of his own Scriptures—the law of faith and practice. And the privilege allowed to other authors of interpreting their own words ought not to be refused to God speaking in the Scriptures.
devotionals.reflection:
This is the heart of the Reformation's answer to Rome, and Turretin's three judges clear up a good deal of confusion.

God speaking in Scripture is the supreme judge, and there is no appeal from him. The church is a real judge under him, like a magistrate who applies a law he did not write. You are a judge too, in a smaller way. You must weigh what you hear and answer for what you believe.

Modern Christians often collapse these. Some make the church supreme. Far more make themselves supreme, with an open Bible and no one who may tell them they are wrong. Turretin leaves no room for either. The Westminster Confession says in its first chapter that the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture is the final judge in every controversy.

Peter says that no prophecy came from human will. The one who gave the Word still explains it, and clearer passages shed light on harder ones.
devotionals.prayer: Sovereign Lord, your Word is final. Let my faith rest on what you have said and on no man's opinion, least of all my own. Give me respect for those who teach me, and give me light on the passages I find hard. Amen.

devotionals.title: No New Word Needed
devotionals.quote: Although the Scriptures cannot hear the arguments of the contending parties (nor always so give its decision as to acquit by name this one and condemn that one), it does not follow that they are not the supreme judge and perfect rule. … It is not necessary for the supreme judge speaking in the Scriptures to declare a new word to us every day on account of new heresies springing up. Hence from the Scriptures, the fathers most triumphantly refuted the heresies of Pelagius, Arius, Macedonius and others, although nothing is said expressly about them.
devotionals.reflection:
The objection was an obvious one. How can a book settle a dispute? It cannot hear the two sides, and it never mentions Arius by name.

Turretin's answer is that no error has ever surprised God. He knew every heresy before he gave his Word, and he wrote with all of them in view. Arius is not named in Scripture, and Scripture answered him. Nicaea was the church reading its Bible carefully.

You will meet questions your grandparents never faced. Your first thought should not be that Christians now need something more. The questions may be new, but God is not behind them. What is needed is patient, faithful reading, and ministers who know their Bibles.

Jude wrote a short letter because error had crept in among believers. He gave them no new revelation. He told them to fight for the faith they had already received. That is still your task.
devotionals.prayer: God of all ages, nothing surprises you. Thank you that your Word is enough for my day. Strengthen faithful ministers who defend it, and give me courage to hold it fast, with gentleness toward those who oppose it. Amen.
